qt: to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:

The sheep and goat pox epizootic in Greece has led to compulsory herd culls and a monthslong ban on the restocking of livestock farms. Affected farmers are deprived not only of their livestock but also of any possibility of finding gainful employment. Exceptional compensation for culled animals does not replace a permanent income replacement mechanism. Meanwhile, professional farmers and livestock farmers who are insured by e-EFKA and previously by the former agricultural insurance organisation (OGA), are not eligible for unemployment benefits for self-employed persons, unlike other categories of self-employed persons. Council Recommendation 2019/C-387/01 includes unemployment benefits in the field of social protection and calls on Member States to ensure effective coverage for the selfemployed. In Spain, the fifth additional provision of Royal Decree 1541/2011 explicitly recognises the period of eradication of a disease in livestock farms as a temporary cessation of activity that is eligible for coverage. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
When monitoring the implementation of Recommendation 2019/C-387/01, did it assess the exclusion of persons insured by the former OGA from unemployment protection in Greece?

Does it believe that the Spanish system can be a good practice for providing coverage to farmers and livestock farmers who are forced to temporarily stop working due to the outbreak of an animal disease?

Does it intend to call on Greece to set up a dedicated unemployment fund for farmers and livestock farmers and point to the available European financial or technical tools that could support its creation and operation?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.11.2026) The Commission supports Member States in implementing the 2019 Council Recommendation on access to social protection which aims to ensure that all workers and self-employed persons have access to adequate social protection, including as regards unemployment benefits. The 2025 update of the monitoring framework1 for this Recommendation identifies for Greece that farmers (registered under former agricultural insurance organisation (OGA) scheme) are not covered for unemployment benefits. These findings are informing the European Semester economic monitoring framework. The 2026 country report for Greece2 notably highlights that access to social protection remains markedly unequal across population groups, particularly among licensed/regulated professions, small business owners, craftspeople, freelancers and farmers. In accordance with Article 153 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, the design and organisation of social protection systems, including conditions for entitlement to benefits, are the competence of Member States. Member States have different approaches to addressing the economic consequences of animal disease outbreaks for farmers and livestock farmers (e.g. recognising temporary cessation of activity as a qualifying situation for social protection benefits, in Spain, or specific income support measures linked to animal disease control, in Ireland). Such arrangements may provide useful examples for consideration by other Member States, but the Commission cannot recommend a specific design for social protection scheme. Lastly, the income support under Common Agriculture Policy provides a certain cushion against income shocks by means of the annual basic income support for sustainability3.
